If you're wondering...

Why would flowers grow among vegetables?

A flower among the rows of carrots seems unnecessary at first glance — it doesn't put anything on your plate, and it takes up space that could just as easily have gone to an extra zucchini. Anyone who views a vegetable garden purely as production space quickly sees a flower as wasted space. But that math only works if you look at the garden as a collection of separate plants, rather than the system it actually is.

The most direct reason is pollination. Zucchini, pumpkin, beans, strawberries, fruit trees: a significant part of your harvest only happens if a pollinator has visited the flower of that plant first. Bees, bumblebees, and hoverflies don't automatically show up in your garden for a single crop that happens to bloom briefly — they need a steady supply, spread out over the season. Flowers among the vegetables provide that supply, and in doing so attract the very pollinators your vegetables need to set fruit.

Flowering herbs also do something else: they attract not only pollinators but also predatory insects and parasitic wasps — the natural enemies of the aphids and caterpillars that do threaten your crops. A flowering border or a few scattered flowering plants between the rows acts as an invitation to the insect army that keeps your pests under control, without you having to do anything yourself.

On top of that, flowers simply increase the diversity of the system, and diversity is exactly the principle a chaos garden runs on: the more species, the more combinations are possible, the more resilient the whole becomes against diseases and pests that target a single species. And then there's the simplest argument of all, one you shouldn't underestimate: a garden with flowers among the greenery is simply more beautiful to stand in. That's not a side issue — a garden you enjoy spending time in is a garden you'll visit, tend, and harvest more often.

A flower puts less on your plate, but without flowers, a lot of what would be on your plate never gets there at all. They're not decoration — they're the invitation to the insect life that makes your garden work.
